\chapter{But, and Or}
\label{ch:ta-but-and-or}
\hlchaptermodality{76}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can set one statement against another, offer a choice between two, and take the answer.}

Complete TA-C76-choice and offer two drinks, in the long form and the short one.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[āṉāl]{\ta{ஆனால்} (āṉāl) — but}

\label{lesson:TA-C76-but}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{சரியா}}. Then ask to be let inside.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஆனால்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}} (\emph{āṉāl}) — \textquotedblleft{}but\textquotedblright{}.

Chapter seventy-four joined two \textbf{things}. This joins two \textbf{statements}, and unlike -\ta{உம்} it is a word of its own, standing between them.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டும்}, \ta{ஆனால்} \ta{பால்} \ta{வேண்டாம்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{tēnīr vēṇḍum, āṉāl pāl vēṇḍām.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}I want tea, but I don't want milk.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Both halves are sentences you could already say. \ta{ஆனால்} sets the second against the first.

The word is built out of \ta{ஆகு}, \textquotedblleft{}to become\textquotedblright{}: \ta{ஆனால்} began as \textquotedblleft{}if that is so\textquotedblright{}. A sentence that starts by granting the first half and then turns is exactly what \emph{but} does.

In everyday speech the tail wears down and you will hear \textbf{\ta{ஆனா}}. It is the same word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two sentences held together, with the second one pushing back.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{āṉāl}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tēnīr vēṇḍum, āṉāl pāl vēṇḍām}
  \item \emph{Build:} \emph{idu nalla vīḍu, āṉāl siṟiya vīḍu}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{சரியா}}, then ask \emph{varalāmā?}, then say \emph{āṉāl}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{-um … -um illai}, \emph{maṭṭum} and \emph{kōpam} — three distances back — then set two of them against each other with \ta{ஆனால்}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What sits between the two halves, and what does the second half do? (\textbf{\ta{ஆனால்} — and the second half turns against the first.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[alladu]{\ta{அல்லது} (alladu) — or}

\label{lesson:TA-C76-or}



\begin{quote}
Ask to be let inside. Then say \emph{but} in Tamil.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{அல்லது}}
\textbf{\ta{அல்லது}} (\emph{alladu}) — \textquotedblleft{}or\textquotedblright{}.

Like \ta{ஆனால்}, it is a word of its own and it stands between the two things it offers.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பால்} \ta{அல்லது} \ta{தேநீர்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{pāl alladu tēnīr.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Milk or tea.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Look at the shape of the word. \textbf{\ta{அது}} is \textquotedblleft{}that one\textquotedblright{}, which you have had since chapter forty; \textbf{\ta{அல்ல}} is a denial. \ta{அல்லது} is \textquotedblleft{}it is not that\textquotedblright{} — and a list that says \emph{this, or if not that} is an offer of a choice.

So Tamil's \emph{and} is an ending, and Tamil's \emph{or} is a small denial. Neither one is the word English would have led you to expect.

It works on two statements as well as two things:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{நீங்கள்} \ta{வரலாம்}, \ta{அல்லது} \ta{நான்} \ta{வருகிறேன்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}You may come, or I will come.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two joins in two lessons: one that sets things against each other, one that offers a choice.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{alladu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pāl alladu tēnīr}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{pālum tēnīrum} against \emph{pāl alladu tēnīr} — both, then either
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{varalāmā?}, then say \emph{āṉāl}, then say \emph{alladu}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{-ā}, \emph{iṉṉum} and \emph{payam} — three distances back — then offer two of them with \ta{அல்லது}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Offer somebody milk or tea. (\textbf{\ta{பால்} \ta{அல்லது} \ta{தேநீர்}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[āṉāl]{\ta{ஆனால்} — three shapes, all of them old}

\label{lesson:TA-W31-read-aanaal}



\begin{quote}
Before the page: say \emph{but}, then say \emph{or}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ta{ஆனால்} — the same long sound, written two ways}
Read it in three pieces.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{ஆ}} & \emph{ā} & the free-standing long vowel, because the word opens on it \\
\textbf{\ta{னா}} & \emph{ṉā} & \ta{ன} with the long \textbf{\ta{ா}} sign \\
\textbf{\ta{ல்}} & \emph{l} & \ta{ல} with a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}, so it carries no vowel \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{ஆ} · \ta{னா} · \ta{ல்} $\to$ \ta{ஆனால்}}
\end{quote}

One word, and the long \emph{ā} appears twice in it — first as a whole letter, then as a sign. That is the rule from \textbf{\ta{இன்று}} and \textbf{\ta{ஆம்}} shown twice inside a single word: at the front of a word a vowel needs its own shape, and anywhere after a consonant it becomes a mark.

The word ends on a \textbf{\ta{புள்ளி}}, and that closing \ta{ல்} is the piece everyday speech drops when it says \textbf{\ta{ஆனா}}.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ஆ}} — then \textbf{\ta{னா}} — then \textbf{\ta{ல்}}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}
  \item \emph{Point to:} the two places the long ā is written, and say why they differ
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{āṉāl}, then say \emph{alladu}, then read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}
  \item \emph{Return to:} say \emph{ām / illai}, say \emph{sīkkiram} and read \textbf{\ta{பயம்}} — three distances back — then offer two of them with \ta{அல்லது}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is the first ā a letter and the second a sign? (\textbf{Because the word begins with the first one, and the second sits on \ta{ன}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pāl vēṇḍumā, alladu tēnīr vēṇḍumā?]{\ta{பால்} \ta{வேண்டுமா}, \ta{அல்லது} \ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டுமா}? — offering a choice}

\label{lesson:TA-C76-choice}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}. Then say \emph{or}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: two questions, one offer}
\textbf{\ta{பால்} \ta{வேண்டுமா}, \ta{அல்லது} \ta{தேநீர்} \ta{வேண்டுமா}?} \emph{pāl vēṇḍumā, alladu tēnīr vēṇḍumā?} — \textquotedblleft{}Would you like milk, or would you like tea?\textquotedblright{}

Every piece is yours. \ta{வேண்டும்} is \textquotedblleft{}want\textquotedblright{}, from chapter thirty-nine. The \textbf{-\ta{ஆ}} on the end of each half is last chapter's question ending. \ta{அல்லது} sits between them.

Notice what Tamil does not do: it does not ask one question with two answers in it. It asks \textbf{two whole questions} and puts \emph{or} between them. Each half could stand alone.

The shorter form drops the second verb, and a host at a doorway will say it that way:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{பால்} \ta{அல்லது} \ta{தேநீர்}?}
\end{quote}

Answer it with the echo you learned for any yes-or-no question — name the one you want:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{தேநீர்}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can put a choice in front of somebody and take their answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Offer:} \emph{pāl vēṇḍumā, alladu tēnīr vēṇḍumā?}
  \item \emph{Offer short:} \emph{pāl alladu tēnīr?}
  \item \emph{Answer:} name one of them
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{alladu}, then read \textbf{\ta{ஆனால்}}, then make the full offer
  \item \emph{Return to:} read \textbf{\ta{சரியா}}, say \emph{uṭaṉē} and say \emph{varuttam} — three distances back — then offer two of them with \ta{அல்லது}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many questions does Tamil ask when it offers two things? (\textbf{Two — one for each, with \ta{அல்லது} between.})
\end{tcolorbox}
